If your working directory is myfolder/homework/, what relative path would you specify to get the file located at myfolder/MyData.csv? The relative path for this file is “../MyData.csv”, where the “..” indicates moving up one directory from the current “homework” folder before accessing “MyData.csv”.
What are the major benefits of using R projects? R projects help keep analyses organized by giving each project its own working directory, workspace, history, folder structure, and source documents. They also make it easier to use relative file paths, which improves reproducibility and facilitates collaboration by enabling running the same code on different computers/by different users.
What is Git and what is GitHub? Git is a version control system that tracks changes made to files over time. It allows users to save versions of their work, review changes, and collaborate without losing previous versions. GitHub is an online platform that hosts Git repositories. It allows users to store their projects remotely, share them with others, collaborate on the same files, and manage changes through tools such as commits, branches, and pull requests.
What are the two main differences between a tibble and a data.frame? A tibble is a special type of data frame. It has additional classes (eg, tbl_df and tbl) while still inheriting from data.frame, so it can generally be used anywhere a regular data frame can be used. Additionally, tibble has a different default printing behavior, where when printed it shows the dimensions, variable types, and only rows/columns that fit reasonably on the screen rather than flooding the console with the entire output.

Task 4: Writing a Function

8. Writing the getIQR() Function
The “getIQR()” function calculates the interquartile range as a difference between the 75th and 25th percentile. Additional arguments can be used to pass unnamed arguments into the quantile function.

# Define a function, calculate the 25th and 75th percentiles, and return difference without a name
getIQR <- function (x, ...) {
  quartiles <- quantile(x, probs = c(0.25, 0.75), ...)
  unname(quartiles[2] - quartiles[1])
}



9. Applying getIQR() Function
The getIQR function written in part 8 of this task is applied separately to “fixed_acidity” and “citric_acid” variables in the combined wine data.

10. Writing the getCoefVar() function
The “getCoefVar()” function calculates the coefficient of variation, defined as the sample standard deviation divided by the absolute value of the sample mean. Additional arguments can be used to pass unnamed arguments into the coefficient of variation function.

# Define a function, calculate sample standard deviation divided by absolute sample mean
getCoefVar <- function (x, ...) {
  sd(x, ...) / abs(mean(x, ...))
}

12. Writing the getSummaries() Function
The “getSummaries()” function returns both the interquartile range and coefficient of variation for a numeric vector. The function uses the previously defined functions from part 8 and 10 of this task, and returns named values for each summary.

# Define a function to return both IQR and coefficient of variation
getSummaries <- function(x, ...) {
  c(
    IQR = getIQR(x, ...),
    CoefVar = getCoefVar(x, ...)
  )
}

R projects give you a way to organize all the things you’re doing in R. I don’t have a ton of experience using them yet, but it seems like they enable you to create an all-inclusive environment for whatever you’re working on at the time. This, in turn, leaves anything else you might be working on in parallel alone. It also lets you tell R where to look when calling files (handy) and helps R communicate with GitHub. Having R projects also lets you switch between broader tasks you might be working on easily in that when you which R projects, everything you need comes with it.



Git is version control software that allows you to save and track changes to files you might be working on, keeping everything in a repository. GitHub is the online service tracks these changes and makes it possible to share your repository so others can colloborate with you and see the changes you’re making.



A tibble is a special, updated version of a data frame which is used within the set of tidyverse packages. One difference between the two is that tibbles print more neatly and show information regarding the number of rows and columns. Another important difference is that data frames convert columns you pull from it to a vector, whereas tibbles continue to treat these as tibbles, which is good because, within the tidyverse, functions are written to take in and output tibbles.

For this task, we’ll start creating functions. To begin, we’ll take in a vector and find the IQR.

getIQR<-function(x){
  quantile(x,0.75,names=0)-quantile(x,0.25,names=0)
}

Note the changing of the names default within the quantiles function so that only the answer is returned. Let’s try it!
